Which Azure Functions hosting plan does Microsoft now recommend for serverless apps?
Flex Consumption: Linux-only, scales to zero, supports VNet integration and optional always-ready instances. The classic Consumption plan is legacy.
A function app must reach VNet resources, scale to zero when idle, and avoid most cold starts, at serverless pricing. Which Azure Functions plan?
Flex Consumption with always-ready instances. Classic Consumption has no VNet integration; Premium does, but always bills for at least one instance.
An Azure Functions app must run in a custom Linux container with no cold starts and VNet access. Which hosting plan should you choose?
Premium plan (Dedicated or Container Apps hosting also work). Flex Consumption and Consumption don't run containers.
A function workflow must call several functions in sequence, fan out over 1,000 files in parallel, then aggregate, keeping state between steps. What should you use?
Durable Functions: an orchestrator using function chaining and fan-out/fan-in, with state checkpointed between steps.
Why must Durable Functions orchestrator code be deterministic?
The orchestrator is replayed from its saved history after each await, so it must take the same path every time. Use the context's time and activity calls, not the system clock or random values.
Durable Functions: an approval waits for a manager and escalates if there is no response within 72 hours. Which pattern?
Human interaction: wait for an external event, raced against a durable timer that triggers the escalation.
Durable Functions monitor or async HTTP API pattern: which polls an external condition on a schedule until it is met?
Monitor. The async HTTP API pattern returns 202 with a status URL that the client polls for a long-running operation.
Logic Apps Consumption or Standard: which supports VNet integration, private endpoints and several workflows in one resource?
Logic Apps Standard: single-tenant, runs on the Functions runtime, billed by hosting plan, and also supports stateless workflows.
A team needs a simple integration (file lands in SharePoint, post to Teams) a few hundred times a month at lowest cost, with no infrastructure. Which Logic Apps option?
Logic Apps Consumption: multitenant and billed per action run, so low volume costs almost nothing. Standard carries a fixed hosting cost.
Azure Functions or Logic Apps: which fits integrating SaaS apps with minimal code using prebuilt connectors?
Logic Apps: designer-first workflows with hundreds of connectors. Functions suits custom code reacting to events.
A Monte Carlo simulation runs thousands of independent tasks on hundreds of VMs, scaling the pool up for the job and to zero afterwards. Which Azure service?
Azure Batch: it manages the VM pool, task scheduling, retries and autoscale, so you don't write a scheduler on top of scale sets.
In Azure Batch, how do you cut cost with interruptible nodes now that low-priority VMs are retired?
Spot nodes, which need a Batch account in user subscription pool allocation mode. Low-priority VMs retired on 30 Sep 2025.
A tightly coupled CFD simulation using MPI needs low-latency node-to-node links. Which Azure VM type should you use?
H-series HPC VMs (HB, HC, HX) with InfiniBand RDMA and inter-node communication enabled. General-purpose D-series has no InfiniBand.
Azure Batch pool allocation: in which mode does Batch create the VMs in your own subscription, under your own core quotas?
User subscription mode, which Spot nodes require. In Batch service mode the VMs live in Batch-managed subscriptions under Batch quotas.
An App Service app must be fully network-isolated on dedicated single-tenant infrastructure at very high scale. What should you recommend?
App Service Environment v3 with Isolated v2 plans, deployed into a subnet of your VNet (internal or external).
An App Service app on a Premium plan only needs outbound access to resources in a VNet. ASE v3 or VNet integration?
VNet integration: it covers outbound traffic far more cheaply. Add a private endpoint for private inbound; ASE is for full single-tenant isolation.
What is the maximum function timeout on the Azure Functions Consumption plan?
10 minutes (default 5). Flex Consumption, Premium and Dedicated default to 30 minutes and can be unbounded.
Why can't an HTTP-triggered Azure Function run a 10-minute job and return the result in the response, even on Premium?
The front-end load balancer times out after about 230 seconds. Use the Durable Functions async HTTP pattern: return 202 with a status URL.
Azure Functions must run alongside other microservices with shared networking, Dapr and KEDA scaling in one environment. Which Functions hosting option?
Azure Container Apps hosting: Linux containers that share the Container Apps environment's networking, KEDA scaling and Dapr.
An AKS cluster occasionally needs hundreds of extra pods within seconds without adding nodes. What can you use?
AKS virtual nodes, which place pods on Azure Container Instances in seconds. The cluster autoscaler adds VMs, which takes minutes.
A web app runs 24x7 at steady load on D-series VMs in one region for the next 3 years. What gives the lowest compute cost?
3-year reserved VM instances, plus Azure Hybrid Benefit for owned licences. A savings plan is more flexible but discounts less for a fixed size and region.
Azure Container Apps: how do you run a canary or blue/green deployment?
Multiple revision mode with percentage traffic splitting between revisions; labels give a revision its own URL for testing.
Containers must process messages from a queue and scale on queue length, including to zero. Which Azure compute should you recommend?
Azure Container Apps with a KEDA queue scale rule (or an event-driven Container Apps job). ACI has no autoscale; AKS works but needs cluster management.
Storage queues or Service Bus queues: an app needs FIFO ordering, duplicate detection, transactions and dead-lettering. Which?
Azure Service Bus. Storage queues offer none of these; they suit simple, very large backlogs.
Maximum message size: Azure Storage queues {{c1::64 KB}}; Service Bus Standard {{c2::256 KB}}; Service Bus Premium {{c3::100 MB}}.
An app must queue more than 80 GB of messages under 64 KB each, needing only simple at-least-once processing at lowest cost. Which service?
Azure Storage queues: they grow to the storage account limit, while a Service Bus queue tops out at 80 GB.

Azure Service Bus tiers: {{c1::Basic}} has queues only; {{c2::Standard}} adds topics, sessions, transactions and duplicate detection; {{c3::Premium}} adds dedicated messaging units, private endpoints and messages up to 100 MB.
A Service Bus namespace must be reachable only through a private endpoint, with predictable latency. Which tier?
Premium: the only tier with private endpoints and dedicated messaging units.
Each order is published once, and billing, shipping and analytics each need their own copy, filtered by order type. What should you use?
A Service Bus topic with one subscription per service, each with a SQL or correlation filter. Needs Standard or Premium.
Service Bus queue or topic: which gives every subscriber its own copy of each message?
Topic (pub/sub). On a queue, receivers compete and each message goes to one consumer.
Messages for the same customer must be processed in order and by one receiver at a time. Which Service Bus feature?
Message sessions: set a SessionId per customer on a session-enabled entity; each session is locked to one receiver and delivered in order.
In Azure Service Bus, where does a message go after repeated processing failures or expiry?
The entity's dead-letter queue: after MaxDeliveryCount (default 10), on TTL expiry if enabled, or when dead-lettered explicitly. You must read and resubmit it yourself.
A sender may retry after network failures and send the same message twice. How can Azure Service Bus discard the duplicates?
Duplicate detection: a repeated MessageId inside the detection window is dropped. Enable it when creating the queue or topic (Standard or Premium).
Event or message in Azure messaging: which carries data the producer expects a consumer to act on?
A message (Service Bus). An event only reports that something happened, with no expectation about handling (Event Grid, Event Hubs).
Azure Event Grid delivers {{c1::discrete}} events by {{c2::push}}; Azure Event Hubs ingests event {{c3::streams}} that consumers {{c4::pull}} from partitions.
When a blob is uploaded, a function must run at once to make a thumbnail, with push delivery and no polling. Which service routes the notification?
Azure Event Grid: a Blob Storage system topic pushes the BlobCreated event to a function subscription.
Millions of telemetry events per second must be ingested, kept for replay, and read by several independent consumers. What should you use?
Azure Event Hubs: partitions for scale, retention for replay, and a consumer group per independent reader.
Event Hubs or IoT Hub: which do you need for device management and cloud-to-device messages?
IoT Hub. It also exposes an Event Hubs-compatible endpoint for the telemetry.
What is the cheapest Azure Event Hubs tier that supports Capture and the Kafka endpoint?
Standard (Capture is a paid add-on there). Basic supports neither.
All events from an event hub must be archived to Azure Data Lake Storage for later batch analytics, without writing code. Which feature?
Event Hubs Capture: writes Avro files to Blob Storage or ADLS Gen2 on a time or size window.
A company runs Apache Kafka producers and consumers and wants a managed Azure service without rewriting client code. What do you recommend?
The Event Hubs Kafka endpoint (Standard tier or higher): change only the connection config. An event hub maps to a Kafka topic.
What sets parallelism and ordering in Azure Event Hubs?
Partitions: order holds only within a partition, and more partitions allow more parallel readers. A partition key such as device ID keeps related events together.
A company wants to publish backend APIs to partners with subscription keys, rate limiting, a developer portal and request transformation. What should you recommend?
Azure API Management. Front Door and Application Gateway route traffic but don't productize APIs.
API Management must be deployed across several Azure regions with one management plane, injected into a VNet and zone-redundant. Which tier?
Premium (classic): the only tier with multi-region deployment. Premium v2 has VNet injection and zones, but no multi-region yet.
Which API Management v2 tier is the lowest with full VNet injection for private inbound and outbound traffic?
Premium v2. Standard v2 offers only outbound VNet integration plus an inbound private endpoint.
APIs run on-premises and in another cloud; their traffic must stay local but be managed from one Azure APIM instance. What should you deploy?
The APIM self-hosted gateway: a container on Kubernetes or Docker near the backends that pulls config from Azure and reports telemetry back.
Which API Management tier fits unpredictable, low-volume traffic with serverless pay-per-call billing?
Consumption: serverless and autoscaling, but no VNet support and possible cold starts.
An APIM API must reject requests that lack a valid Entra ID token. Which inbound policy do you add?
validate-jwt (or validate-azure-ad-token for Entra-specific checks).
An APIM API must limit each subscription to 100 calls per minute. Which policy do you add?
rate-limit (or rate-limit-by-key). Use quota for longer-period caps such as calls per month.
In the cache-aside pattern with Azure Managed Redis, what does the app do on a cache miss?
Loads the item from the data store, writes it into the cache, then returns it. On updates it writes to the store and invalidates the cached entry.
You need a new Redis cache today for session state and caching. Which Azure product should you recommend?
Azure Managed Redis. Azure Cache for Redis is retiring (Basic/Standard/Premium on 30 Sep 2028) and new customers can no longer create it.

Azure Managed Redis tiers: memory-heavy, low throughput → {{c1::Memory Optimized}}; general workloads → {{c2::Balanced}}; maximum throughput → {{c3::Compute Optimized}}; very large datasets cheaply on RAM plus NVMe → {{c4::Flash Optimized}}.
A global app needs a Redis cache in several regions where each region reads and writes locally (active-active). What do you recommend?
Azure Managed Redis with active geo-replication on an in-memory tier. Legacy Azure Cache for Redis Premium offered only passive geo-replication.
Static content for a global website must be cached at the edge near users, combined with WAF and global HTTP load balancing. What should you use?
Azure Front Door Standard or Premium: edge caching, WAF and global layer-7 routing in one service.
Azure App Configuration or Key Vault: where do feature flags and non-secret app settings belong?
App Configuration. Secrets, keys and certificates stay in Key Vault, and App Configuration holds Key Vault references to them.
Microservices on App Service, Functions and AKS need central config changeable without redeploying, plus a feature switched on for 10% of users. What should you use?
Azure App Configuration with a feature flag using a percentage or targeting filter, read through managed identity.
Bicep or Terraform: which should you choose for Azure-only IaC with the simplest syntax and no state file?
Bicep: it compiles to ARM JSON and supports new resource types from day one. Terraform suits multi-cloud with one tool but keeps a state file.
A set of resources must deploy as one managed unit, be protected from changes outside the deployment, and have removed resources cleaned up. What should you use?
Deployment stacks with deny settings (denyDelete or denyWriteAndDelete) and actionOnUnmanage set to delete.
Resource locks or deployment stacks: which also tracks managed resources and deletes ones dropped from the template?
Deployment stacks. Locks only block delete or modify operations.
Code is in GitHub and you need CI/CD that deploys Bicep to Azure without storing long-lived secrets. What should you recommend?
GitHub Actions signing in to Entra ID with OpenID Connect (workload identity federation), then deploying the Bicep. No client secret is stored.
An App Service app needs zero-downtime deployment, validation in staging with production settings, and instant rollback. What should you use?
Deployment slots: deploy to staging, warm up, swap into production, and swap back to roll back. Needs Standard tier or higher.
In App Service, how do you keep a setting such as a staging connection string with its slot during a swap?
Mark it as a deployment slot setting (sticky); it stays with the slot instead of moving with the app.
You want to share a versioned, approved Bicep or ARM template across the organization, with RBAC on who can deploy it. What should you use?
Template specs: versioned Azure resources controlled by RBAC. A private Bicep module registry in ACR is the alternative.
A database is overloaded by repeated identical reads of catalog data that changes hourly. What is the cheapest architectural fix?
A distributed cache (Azure Managed Redis) using cache-aside with a TTL of up to an hour. Scaling up or adding replicas costs more and still hits the database.
Event Grid or Service Bus: a payment service must process each order once, in order, transactionally, with retries over days. Which?
Service Bus: sessions, duplicate detection, transactions and a dead-letter queue. Event Grid retries for only 24 hours by default and has no ordering.
Which Azure messaging service offers an MQTT broker for pub/sub between IoT clients, plus HTTP push delivery?
Event Grid namespaces (MQTT broker feature). IoT Hub also speaks MQTT, but for device-to-cloud traffic with device management.
How can Azure API Management reduce backend load for frequently requested GET responses?
Response caching policies: cache-lookup inbound and cache-store outbound, using the built-in cache or an external Redis-compatible cache.
Cloud Adoption Framework phases in order: {{c1::Strategy}} → {{c2::Plan}} → {{c3::Ready}} → {{c4::Adopt}}, with {{c5::Govern, Secure and Manage}} running continuously.
In which Cloud Adoption Framework phase do you deploy the landing zone (management groups, policy, networking, identity) before migrating?
Ready. Plan comes before it (estate inventory and adoption plan); Adopt comes after (migrate and modernize).
In which Cloud Adoption Framework phase do you record business motivations, such as leaving a datacenter by contract end, and expected outcomes?
Strategy. Plan then turns it into a prioritized backlog.

Cloud rationalization: move the VM as-is = {{c1::Rehost}}; minor changes to adopt PaaS such as SQL MI = {{c2::Refactor (replatform)}}; significant code changes for cloud-native design = {{c3::Rearchitect}}; rewrite from scratch = {{c4::Rebuild}}; swap for SaaS = {{c5::Replace}}.
A company will swap its on-premises CRM for Dynamics 365. Which Cloud Adoption Framework rationalization strategy is that?
Replace: the workload is swapped for a SaaS product.
A company must vacate its datacenter in 4 months and move apps with minimal changes. Which migration strategy and tool?
Rehost (lift-and-shift) with the Azure Migrate Migration and modernization tool; modernize after the exit.
Which Azure tool discovers on-premises VMware, Hyper-V and physical servers, assesses readiness, right-sizes, estimates cost and then migrates them?
Azure Migrate: its appliance does discovery, Discovery and assessment sizes and prices, and Migration and modernization moves the servers.
What does the Azure Migrate appliance do?
Discovers on-premises servers and collects config, performance, software inventory and dependency data, sending the metadata to the Azure Migrate project. It also drives agentless VMware replication.
You must find which servers talk to each other so dependent servers migrate together, without installing anything on them. What should you use?
Agentless dependency analysis in Azure Migrate, collected by the appliance. The agent-based option needs agents and Log Analytics.
Azure Migrate server migration: when do you need agent-based replication instead of agentless?
For physical servers, AWS or GCP VMs and other hypervisors, or VMs that fail agentless prerequisites. Agentless is the default for VMware and Hyper-V.
Online or offline database migration: which keeps downtime to the final cutover?
Online: data syncs continuously and the app stops only at cutover. Offline downtime starts when the migration starts.
50 SQL Server databases must move to Azure SQL Managed Instance with minimal downtime through a managed, at-scale migration pipeline. What should you use?
Azure Database Migration Service in online mode, run from the portal, PowerShell or CLI. The Managed Instance link is a near-zero-downtime alternative.
SQL Data Migration Assistant (DMA) is retired. Which tools replace it for assessing and migrating SQL Server to Azure?
Azure Migrate or SQL Server enabled by Azure Arc for assessment, and Azure DMS for the migration. DMA retired on 16 July 2025.
An Oracle, Db2, MySQL or SAP ASE database must move to Azure SQL. Which tool converts its schema and code?
SQL Server Migration Assistant (SSMA) for that source platform. DMS and Azure Migrate handle SQL Server sources only.
Azure Data Box sizing per order: under ~40 TB → {{c1::Data Box Disk}}; 40–480 TB → {{c2::Data Box 120}}; more than 480 TB → {{c3::Data Box 525}}.
A Data Box Disk order is up to five 8 TB disks, about 35 TB usable.
A company must copy 300 TB to Azure over a 100 Mbps link within 4 weeks. What should you recommend?
Azure Data Box (for example three Data Box 120 devices). At 100 Mbps, 300 TB would take about nine months online.
Which tool fits a scripted one-off or incremental copy of about 1 TB from local disk or S3 into Azure Blob Storage over a good link?
AzCopy: command-line copy over HTTPS with sync, using SAS or Entra auth. Storage Mover suits managed NAS migrations; Data Box is offline.
Branch offices need fast local file share access while the full dataset lives in Azure Files, with cold files tiered to the cloud. What should you use?
Azure File Sync: an agent on Windows Server caches hot files locally and tiers cold files to Azure Files.
Azure File Sync or Azure Storage Mover: which gives an ongoing on-premises cache of Azure Files?
Azure File Sync. Storage Mover is a migration tool, not a hybrid cache.
Many on-premises NAS SMB and NFS shares (millions of files) must move to Azure Files or Blob, fully managed from Azure, with metadata fidelity and repeatable jobs. What should you use?
Azure Storage Mover: agents near the source run job definitions managed centrally in Azure.
A 400 TB NAS must move to Azure over a slow link and stay in sync until cutover. Which combination should you recommend?
Data Box for the bulk seed, then Storage Mover for the deltas.
Azure Import/Export or Data Box: which has you ship your own disk drives?
Import/Export: your own SATA HDDs or SSDs, BitLocker-encrypted and prepared with the WAImportExport tool. Data Box uses Microsoft-supplied devices.
An IIS-hosted .NET web app should move to PaaS with minimal code changes after a compatibility assessment. Which tool?
Azure Migrate web app discovery and assessment, then migration to App Service. This is replatforming, not a rehost.
Which Azure Migrate assessment sizing sizes VMs from measured CPU, memory and disk use over time rather than allocated resources?
Performance-based sizing. As-on-premises copies the allocated size. Collect at least a week of data, ideally a month, for good confidence.
A SQL Server instance uses cross-database queries, SQL Agent jobs and CLR and must move to PaaS with minimal changes. Which target?
Azure SQL Managed Instance: near-full instance compatibility. Azure SQL Database lacks SQL Agent and cross-database queries.

Azure load balancing: regional layer 4 = {{c1::Load Balancer}}; regional layer 7 with WAF = {{c2::Application Gateway}}; global layer 7 with edge caching = {{c3::Front Door}}; global DNS-based for any protocol = {{c4::Traffic Manager}}.
A public web app runs in two regions and needs global HTTPS routing to the nearest healthy region, TLS offload, path routing, WAF and edge caching. What should you use?
Azure Front Door (Premium for Private Link origins). Traffic Manager is DNS-only, with no TLS offload, caching or WAF; Application Gateway is regional.
A non-HTTP service, such as a TCP game server, runs in several regions and clients must reach the nearest healthy one. What fits?
Traffic Manager (DNS, any protocol) or the Global Load Balancer (layer 4, anycast IP). Front Door and Application Gateway are HTTP(S) only.
Traffic Manager or the cross-region Global Load Balancer: which fails over without waiting for DNS TTL?
Global Load Balancer: one static anycast IP that preserves client IP. Its backends must be regional Standard Load Balancers.
Traffic Manager routing: active/passive failover = {{c1::Priority}}; split traffic by percentage = {{c2::Weighted}}; lowest latency = {{c3::Performance}}.
Traffic Manager routing: route by user location for data sovereignty = {{c1::Geographic}}; return several healthy endpoints = {{c2::MultiValue}}; map client IP ranges to endpoints = {{c3::Subnet}}.
A regional web app needs path-based routing, TLS termination, cookie affinity, autoscaling, zone redundancy and OWASP protection inside a VNet. What should you use?
Application Gateway v2 with WAF (WAF_v2 SKU and a WAF policy). v1 retired on 28 Apr 2026.
SQL Server Always On or a TCP line-of-business app on VMs needs highly available load balancing on a private IP within one region. What should you use?
An internal Standard Load Balancer (layer 4). Application Gateway is HTTP(S) only; Traffic Manager and Front Door are global.
What happened to the Azure Basic Load Balancer and Basic public IP SKUs?
Retired on 30 Sep 2025; use Standard, which is zone-redundant and closed to inbound traffic unless an NSG allows it.
What changed for outbound internet access in new Azure VNets created with API versions released after 31 March 2026?
Their subnets default to private, with no default outbound access. VMs need explicit egress: NAT Gateway, Load Balancer outbound rules or a public IP. Existing VNets are unchanged.
Hundreds of VMs in private subnets need reliable outbound internet through fixed public IPs, without SNAT port exhaustion or inbound exposure. What should you use?
Azure NAT Gateway on the subnets, with public IPs or a prefix: outbound-only, and it takes precedence over other outbound methods.
Outbound traffic from private subnets also needs FQDN filtering and inspection. What do you add beyond NAT Gateway?
Azure Firewall, with UDRs sending egress through it. NAT Gateway can sit on the firewall subnet for SNAT scale.

Azure Firewall SKUs: {{c1::Basic}} for small businesses up to 250 Mbps; {{c2::Standard}} adds web categories, DNS proxy and threat-intel deny up to 30 Gbps; {{c3::Premium}} adds TLS inspection, IDPS and URL filtering up to 100 Gbps.
Outbound HTTPS must be decrypted and checked for malware signatures, and specific URL paths (not just domains) blocked. What do you need?
Azure Firewall Premium with TLS inspection, IDPS and URL filtering. Standard filters by FQDN only and can't decrypt TLS.
NSG or Azure Firewall: which centrally filters by FQDN, with threat intelligence, across VNets?
Azure Firewall, usually in the hub. NSGs are free layer 3/4 allow/deny rules on subnets or NICs; most designs use both.
Web and DB VMs share a subnet; you want to allow web tier to DB tier on 1433 without maintaining IP addresses in rules. What should you use?
Application security groups referenced in NSG rules, grouping NICs by role. Members must be in the same VNet.
Azure WAF on Front Door or on Application Gateway: which fits a regional, internal-only web app?
Application Gateway, inside your VNet. WAF on Front Door protects global public apps at the edge.
DDoS Network Protection or DDoS IP Protection: which adds rapid response support, cost protection and a WAF discount?
Network Protection: one plan covering up to 100 public IPs. IP Protection is billed per IP, with the same mitigation but none of those extras.
A company with 3 public IPs needs adaptive DDoS mitigation and attack metrics, but not rapid response or cost protection. What is the cheapest option?
DDoS IP Protection on each IP. The Network Protection plan's fixed monthly cost only pays off with many IPs (about 15 or more) or when you need its extras.
Private endpoint or service endpoint: which gives the PaaS resource a private IP in your VNet?
Private endpoint (Private Link): reachable from peered VNets and on-premises, and public access can be disabled. A service endpoint still targets the public endpoint.
On-premises servers must reach an Azure Storage account privately over ExpressRoute. Service endpoint or private endpoint?
Private endpoint: service endpoints work only from subnets inside Azure VNets.
After creating a private endpoint for a storage account, VMs still resolve its public IP. What is missing?
A private DNS zone such as privatelink.blob.core.windows.net, linked to the VNet, holding the endpoint's A record.
On-premises clients must resolve an Azure private endpoint name. Where should on-premises DNS forward the query?
To an Azure DNS Private Resolver inbound endpoint (or a DNS forwarder VM in Azure), which asks Azure DNS at 168.63.129.16.
As a SaaS provider, you want customers to connect privately from their own VNets to your service behind a Standard Load Balancer, without peering or IP overlap issues. What should you use?
Azure Private Link service in front of the load balancer; customers create private endpoints to it.
Private endpoint or Private Link service: which one does the service provider create?
Private Link service. The consumer creates the private endpoint that connects to it.
PaaS resources (Storage, Key Vault, SQL, Event Hubs) need a logical boundary that blocks public access, lets members talk to each other and logs access, without VNets. What should you use?
Network security perimeter, rolled out in transition mode first and then switched to enforced mode.
Admins need browser RDP/SSH to VMs with no public IPs; production needs session recording and no public IP on the bastion either. Which Azure Bastion SKU?
Bastion Premium: the only SKU with session recording and private-only deployment.
Admins must use their native RDP/SSH client and transfer files through Azure Bastion, with scaling for many sessions. What is the minimum SKU?
Standard: adds native client support, file transfer and host scaling. Basic is portal-only with two fixed instances.
All internet-bound traffic from spoke VNets must pass through Azure Firewall in the hub. What do you configure?
A UDR on the spoke subnets: 0.0.0.0/0 with next hop virtual appliance, the firewall's private IP. UDRs override system routes.
Policy requires internet traffic from Azure to leave through the on-premises datacenter. What is this design called?
Forced tunneling: a default route advertised from on-premises over BGP, or Azure Firewall in forced tunneling mode, which needs a management subnet.
Site-to-Site VPN, Point-to-Site VPN or ExpressRoute: which gives a private link that avoids the internet, with predictable latency?
ExpressRoute, through a provider (up to 10 Gbps) or ExpressRoute Direct (10, 100 or 400 Gbps ports).
Site-to-Site or Point-to-Site VPN: which connects individual remote laptops rather than a whole branch network?
Point-to-Site (OpenVPN, IKEv2 or SSTP). Site-to-Site links a branch or datacenter over IPsec.
Is Azure ExpressRoute traffic encrypted by default?
No. Add MACsec on ExpressRoute Direct, or run IPsec over private peering, if you need encryption.

ExpressRoute circuit SKUs: {{c1::Local}} reaches only the one or two regions near the peering location; {{c2::Standard}} reaches all regions in the same geopolitical area; {{c3::Premium}} reaches all regions worldwide.
An ExpressRoute circuit in Amsterdam must reach VNets in West US and Australia East. Which circuit SKU?
ExpressRoute Premium: Standard reaches only regions in the same geopolitical area (Europe here).
On-premises datacenters in London and New York each have an ExpressRoute circuit and must talk to each other over the Microsoft backbone. What should you enable?
ExpressRoute Global Reach, which links the two circuits. Not available on Local.
Throughput between on-premises and VMs over ExpressRoute is limited by the gateway. Which feature sends data-path traffic straight to the VMs?
ExpressRoute FastPath: the gateway still exchanges routes, but data bypasses it.
A company needs dual 100 Gbps (or 400 Gbps) links straight into Microsoft's network at a peering location, with no provider, and MACsec. What should you use?
ExpressRoute Direct. Provider circuits top out at 10 Gbps.
How do you make an ExpressRoute connection resilient cost-effectively if the circuit or provider fails?
A Site-to-Site VPN as backup, with VPN and ExpressRoute gateways coexisting in the GatewaySubnet. ExpressRoute routes win; the VPN takes over on failure.
For maximum ExpressRoute resiliency, where should two circuits terminate?
At two different peering locations, so one site outage can't take both down.
Is Azure VNet peering transitive? If spokes A and B both peer with a hub, can A reach B?
No. Route through an NVA or Azure Firewall in the hub with UDRs, peer A and B directly, or use Virtual Network Manager or Virtual WAN.
Spoke VNets must reach on-premises through the hub's VPN or ExpressRoute gateway without their own gateways. Which peering settings do you configure?
Allow gateway transit on the hub side and Use remote gateways on the spoke side.
Hub-spoke or Azure Virtual WAN: which suits many branches across regions with automatic any-to-any transit?
Virtual WAN: Microsoft-managed hubs, SD-WAN integration and transitive routing. A self-built hub-spoke gives full control of the hub VNet.
Which Azure VM feature lowers latency and jitter and raises packets per second by bypassing the host's virtual switch (SR-IOV)?
Accelerated Networking: free, on most sizes with two or more vCPUs.
A latency-sensitive multi-tier app, such as a trading system, needs its VMs physically as close as possible in one datacenter. What should you use?
A proximity placement group, plus Accelerated Networking. The trade-off is fewer allocation options.
A VNet must resolve on-premises DNS names, and on-premises clients must resolve Azure private DNS zones, without running DNS VMs. What should you use?
Azure DNS Private Resolver: an inbound endpoint for on-premises queries into Azure, and an outbound endpoint with a forwarding ruleset for the reverse.
Remote Windows and macOS employees need secure access to Azure VNets with Entra ID sign-in and MFA. What should you configure?
Point-to-Site VPN using OpenVPN with Microsoft Entra ID authentication and the Azure VPN Client; Conditional Access enforces MFA.
An app in a VNet must reach Azure Storage privately, and only one specific storage account may be reachable that way. Service endpoint or private endpoint?
Private endpoint: it maps to one storage account. A service endpoint opens the path to every account unless you add service endpoint policies.
A global HTTP app must be reachable only through Front Door, and its App Service origins must not be publicly reachable. What should you do?
Use Front Door Premium with Private Link origins. Otherwise allow only the AzureFrontDoor.Backend service tag and check the X-Azure-FDID header.
Which VPN gateway SKU family should you choose for production Site-to-Site connectivity?
The zone-redundant AZ SKUs (VpnGw1AZ to VpnGw5AZ), sized by tunnels and throughput. The Basic SKU lacks BGP and active-active.
Global users of a single-region web app see high latency on dynamic, uncacheable API calls. How can Azure Front Door still help?
Edge termination and backbone routing: TCP and TLS end at the nearest edge (split TCP), and requests ride Microsoft's network to the origin.
